source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Explain how RabbitMQ prevents message loss end to end, including the publisher-to-broker path, broker durability/replication, and consumer processing acknowledgements.

claims.text: RabbitMQ message-loss prevention is an end-to-end responsibility split across publisher-to-broker confirmation, broker-side durable/replicated storage, and consumer-side processing acknowledgement; publisher confirms and consumer acknowledgements solve different links and are explicitly orthogonal.
source_anchors: consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms are orthogonal
data safety is shared by publisher broker and consumer

claims.text: A publisher must not equate a successful socket write with broker acceptance. Publisher confirms tell the publisher which publications the broker has accepted; after a connection/channel failure, unconfirmed publications should be retransmitted, which can create duplicates and therefore requires idempotent handling downstream.
source_anchors: retransmit unconfirmed publications after connection failure

claims.text: A publisher confirm alone does not mean a message matched the intended queue. When the application requires detection of unroutable AMQP 0-9-1 publications, it should use the mandatory publishing path and handle basic.return in addition to confirms.

For restart durability with queues, applications use durable queues and persistent publications; a durable queue alone does not make transient messages survive recovery. Publisher confirms are still required to know whether a persistent publication reached the broker's durable acceptance point.

For quorum queues, publisher confirms are tied to quorum replication: a confirmed publication is considered safe once accepted by a quorum, subject to the documented majority-availability assumptions; unconfirmed publications have no such safety guarantee.
source_anchors: unconfirmed publications have no safety guarantee

claims.text: Consumers that require redelivery on failure should use manual acknowledgements and acknowledge only after successful business processing. If a delivery remains unacknowledged when its channel or connection closes, RabbitMQ can requeue/redeliver it; explicit nack/reject controls requeue versus discard/dead-letter behavior.
source_anchors: automatic requeue after channel or connection loss

claims.text: Reliable retry/redelivery paths can produce duplicate deliveries, so 'do not lose messages' is not the same as 'exactly once'. Consumer business effects should be idempotent or deduplicated around a stable business/message identifier.

writer_constraints: Structure the answer by loss boundary: producer -> broker, broker storage/replication, broker -> consumer/business processing.
Do not say that message persistence alone guarantees no loss; pair durability with publisher confirms and the selected queue type's safety semantics.
Do not say publisher confirms prove consumer processing; publisher confirms and consumer acknowledgements are orthogonal.
Do not say a consumer should ack immediately on receipt when business processing still can fail; ack after the intended success boundary.
Explain that retries/redelivery introduce duplicate risk and therefore require idempotent business handling; do not promise exactly-once semantics from RabbitMQ mechanisms alone.
Treat dead-lettering as poison/failure routing, not as an automatic proof of end-to-end no-loss correctness.
Keep quorum-queue guarantees conditional on publisher confirms and majority availability; do not generalize them to every queue type.
Do not fabricate project experience, incident metrics, broker topology, or application-specific retry thresholds.
